title: Sharing Best Practices Across Teams
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece observes a paradox: leaders who are quick to borrow good ideas from anywhere, including competitors, are often reluctant to share their own team's best practices with peer teams inside the same organization. The author attributes this to a form of competitive jealousy, where leaders worry that sharing a distinguishing practice erodes their team's ability to stand out. The recommended fix is structural — a recurring forum where credit and recognition are explicitly attached to cross-team sharing, which realigns incentives toward openness.
points: Leaders often eagerly borrow best practices from outside the organization but resist sharing their own team's practices internally with peer teams.
The reluctance to share stems from competitive jealousy — a fear that visibility and distinctiveness get diluted once a practice spreads.
Creating a recurring forum that explicitly credits teams for sharing best practices realigns incentives so that spreading ideas becomes the way to stand out.
Silos between teams and divisions compound the sharing problem when there's no regular structural occasion for cross-team communication.
quotes: The best team leaders are not bashful about good ideas. They don’t care where a best practice originates.
However, those same leaders seem to rarely look across the aisle for best practices or share what they learn and implement with other teams.
Once this competitive jealousy takes hold, leaders keep their mouths shut and focus inward and not outward.
The best organizations place an emphasis on collaboration by expecting and rewarding it.
It just goes to show that whatever is emphasized and rewarded has a profound effect on team behavior, as well.
